Pulmonology · published research

Diaphragm contractile dysfunction

One LPS-induced rat experiment found that low-level laser treatment partly restored electrically evoked diaphragm force and lowered TNF-alpha compared with untreated injury controls.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One LPS-induced rat experiment found that low-level laser treatment partly restored electrically evoked diaphragm force and lowered TNF-alpha compared with untreated injury controls.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Respiratory system > Diaphragm category contains one experimental rat publication. It studies inflammation-induced contractile dysfunction rather than a diagnosed patient group. No independent human trial, review, or second animal experiment is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

No direct human study of PBM for diaphragm contractile dysfunction was identified in the assigned category.

Animal evidence

Aimbire et al. induced acute lung and diaphragm inflammation in rats with lipopolysaccharide. Low-level laser treatment partly restored electrically evoked diaphragm force and reduced TNF-alpha compared with untreated injury controls (2006). This is one short-duration induced model, not evidence of improved breathing or respiratory failure outcomes in patients.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell, tissue, or ex-vivo diaphragm study is listed. Cytokine measurement in the rat model is an animal outcome, not an in-vitro experiment.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used a 650-nm red laser and reported treatment across four sessions within 24 hours, with a cumulative fluence of 5.2 J/cm2. Wavelength is the color band of the light and influences how it interacts with tissue. The finding applies to this experimental exposure and model only.

Interpretation

The result is a specific preclinical improvement in contractile force and an inflammatory marker. Replication and dose-response work are needed before any clinical inference. A human study would need to measure respiratory muscle strength, breathing support, function, and adverse effects directly.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for improved diaphragm force in an induced rat inflammation model No direct human evidence identified
Publications and records1 title (exact Respiratory system > Diaphragm)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The rating reflects one controlled rat experiment using an acute endotoxin model, with no patient studies and no replication in the assigned category. Independent animal replication with transparent dose reporting should precede clinical research that tests respiratory muscle function and safety in people.
